vignette:
Rohan Patel is a 29-year-old shopowner who came to treatment months after the end of a violent relationship with a former girlfriend who had repeatedly assaulted him behind the counter of the small convenience store he runs. The incident he returns to most often happened late in the evening after closing, when the store was hot, the air stale, and she confronted him over a conversation she had overheard him having with a female supplier. He remembers the sharpness of her voice more than the exact words at first, then the smell of sweat in the cramped space as she shoved him into the shelving and kept demanding answers while he froze. What stays with him is not only the physical force but the humiliating sense that he did nothing effective to stop it. In the months since, certain conversation topics-especially jealousy, cheating, or who someone was talking to-have become charged for him in a way he cannot control.

Now even ordinary moments in the shop can feel dangerous. If a customer steps too close to the counter smelling of sweat or body odor, Rohan feels his body tense before he has time to think, and strangers approaching him can seem immediately threatening even when they are only asking for cigarettes or directions. The same thing happens if customers begin arguing about relationships or accusing one another of lying; by night, when he is locking up and the store is quiet, he feels especially exposed and much less able to believe he is safe. He has trouble falling asleep after late shifts, and when he wakes in the night his mind goes quickly to the sense that something bad could happen again.

These triggers do not just make him anxious; they pull the event back with startling force. A whiff of sweat in a narrow aisle or a sudden argument about infidelity can bring the full memory back without warning, as if the scene is happening in the present rather than the past. At other times there is no clear picture at all-just the same surge of emotional intensity, his chest tight, anger rising instantly, his whole body reacting before he can place why. He says that when the memory does arrive clearly, what he feels most strongly is rage: at her, at the scene, and at himself for standing there and taking it. Because his body reacts so fast and so completely, he has come to believe that his body is an enemy of sorts, still acting as if he is in danger when he knows, rationally, that he is alone in his own store.

That belief has spread into how he sees himself more generally. Rohan is harsh with himself about freezing during the assaults and says he will never forgive himself for not doing more to stop what happened. He has come to doubt his own judgment and steadiness, telling himself he cannot rely on himself if he failed in that moment. Those conclusions make each new jolt of bodily alarm feel like proof rather than symptom: if his pulse jumps when someone comes near, he takes it as evidence that he is still vulnerable and still unable to protect himself. In that state, strangers seem more dangerous, nights feel less safe, and sleep becomes harder to find.

The memories deepen those beliefs. Each time the scene returns with that same helplessness and rage, he reads it as confirmation that he is weak and fundamentally unreliable. And because he is already braced for these reactions, he moves through the store scanning for anything that might set him off-someone sweaty from summer heat, a couple beginning to quarrel near the refrigerator, even his own intrusive thought of the event appearing out of nowhere. The more he anticipates these moments, the more quickly he notices them. A customer's smell can seize his attention instantly; a scrap of conversation can stick in his mind long after the person has left.

Over time this has changed how he works and lives. He keeps interactions brief, becomes guarded with unfamiliar customers, and is especially tense during evening hours. When his partner tries to talk about conflict in relationships, he often shuts the conversation down or goes silent, already feeling the memory stirring and his body turning against him. He is seeking help now because he is exhausted by sleeping badly, by feeling threatened in his own shop, and by how quickly a smell, a topic, or even the sudden arrival of the memory itself can pull him back into rage and self-blame. What frightens him most is the thought that this means he will never be able to trust himself again; what he hopes for, though he says it cautiously, is to be able to stand behind his own counter at night without feeling as if the past is about to happen again.
